marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q019.takeaway: MMC phase III propagates aborally from the duodenum at about 5–10 cm/min during fasting.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q019.displayText:
MMC phase III propagates aborally from the duodenum at about 5–10 cm/min during fasting.

From the duodenum, the migrating motor complex (MMC) moves distally at 5-10 cm/min, reaching the terminal ileum after 1.5 hours.

In the fasting state, there is a period of quiescence in the small bowel, lasting for approximately 40 minutes (phase I). This is followed by a series of waves, also lasting for about 40 minutes, propagating from the fundus of the stomach in a caudal direction at a rate of about 3 per minute (phase II).

Duodenal slow waves are generated in the duodenum at a rate of about 10 per minute, which carry down the small bowel.

The amplitude of these contractions increases to a maximum in phase III, which lasts for about 10 minutes. This 90-minute cycle of activity is then repeated.
emphasis: MMC phase III propagates aborally from the duodenum at about 5–10 cm/min during fasting

rationales.a: The MMC cycle includes phases and recurs about every 90–120 minutes; one phase does not last 50 minutes.
rationales.b: Duodenal slow waves propagate distally and are not limited to the duodenum.
rationales.d: Phase III has strong, maximal contractions rather than minimal amplitude.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q020.takeaway: Secretin reduces small-intestinal motility, while gastroenteric reflexes, CCK and serotonin can increase it.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q020.displayText:
Secretin reduces small-intestinal motility, while gastroenteric reflexes, CCK and serotonin can increase it.

Secretin inhibits small intestinal motility.

Factors that increase the peristaltic activity of the small intestine:
• Hormonal - gastrin, CCK, insulin, motilin, and serotonin
• Neural - duodenal distension by chyme, gastroenteric reflexes, gastroileal reflexes, parasympathetic (ACh) stimulation

Factors that decrease the peristaltic activity of the small intestine:
• Hormonal - secretin and glucagon
• Neural - sympathetic stimulation

Gastroileal reflex: On reaching the ileocecal valve, the chyme is sometimes blocked for several hours until the person eats another meal. At that time, a gastroileal reflex intensifies peristalsis in the ileum and forces the remaining chyme through the ileocecal valve into the cecum of the large intestine.
emphasis: Secretin reduces small-intestinal motility, while gastroenteric reflexes, CCK and serotonin can increase it

rationales.b: The gastroenteric reflex increases intestinal motility after gastric activity.
rationales.c: CCK can stimulate intestinal motility while coordinating digestion.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q021.takeaway: The colon has the longest transit time because water absorption and storage delay onward movement.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q021.displayText:
The colon has the longest transit time because water absorption and storage delay onward movement.

The longest transit time is seen in the colon.

Average transit time is shown in the source table.
emphasis: The colon has the longest transit time because water absorption and storage delay onward movement

rationales.a: Stomach emptying is much faster than whole-colon transit.
rationales.b: Jejunal transit is relatively rapid compared with colonic residence.
rationales.d: Ileal transit is shorter than the prolonged colonic transit.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q022.takeaway: The sigmoid colon shows prominent motility and mass movements before rectal filling and defecation.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q022.displayText:
The sigmoid colon shows prominent motility and mass movements before rectal filling and defecation.

The maximum motility of the colon is seen in the sigmoid colon.

The rate of BER at sigmoid colon is 6/min.
emphasis: The sigmoid colon shows prominent motility and mass movements before rectal filling and defecation

rationales.a: The ascending colon mainly mixes and absorbs; peak distal propulsive activity is later.
rationales.b: Transverse colon participates in propulsion but is not the most motile region in this item.
rationales.c: Descending colon stores/transports contents; sigmoid is the principal distal segment for mass movement.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q023.takeaway: Rectal distension triggers local and sacral reflexes that increase peristalsis in the distal colon.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q023.displayText:
Rectal distension triggers local and sacral reflexes that increase peristalsis in the distal colon.

While doing sigmoidoscopy if the rectum is inflated with gas, increased peristalsis is seen in the distal colon.

The distention of the rectal wall initiates afferent signals. These signals spread through the myenteric plexus to initiate peristaltic waves in the descending colon, sigmoid (distal colon), and rectum.
emphasis: Rectal distension triggers local and sacral reflexes that increase peristalsis in the distal colon

rationales.a: The response is predominantly distal rather than a uniform increase throughout the colon.
rationales.b: Proximal colon is not the main segment responding to rectal distension.
rationales.d: The response is not propagated through the whole intestine.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q024.takeaway: Meissner (submucosal) plexuses primarily regulate gastrointestinal secretion and local blood flow.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q024.displayText:
Meissner (submucosal) plexuses primarily regulate gastrointestinal secretion and local blood flow.

Secretions of GIT are controlled by the Meissner plexus.
emphasis: Meissner (submucosal) plexuses primarily regulate gastrointestinal secretion and local blood flow

rationales.b: Auerbach is another name for myenteric plexus and primarily regulates movement.
rationales.d: Extrinsic nerves modulate GI function but local secretion control is assigned to Meissner plexus.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q025.takeaway: The first urge to defecate is felt when rectal pressure reaches about 18 mmHg.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q025.displayText:
The first urge to defecate is felt when rectal pressure reaches about 18 mmHg.

The first urge to defecate occurs when rectal pressure is increased to 18 mm Hg.

When this pressure reaches 55 mm Hg, the external and the internal sphincter relax, and there is reflex expulsion of the contents of the rectum.

Defecation reflex: Distension of the rectum and colon stimulates stretch receptors in the rectal wall. Then, the defecation reflex travels from the colon and rectum to the spinal cord and back again to produce the powerful colonic, rectal, and abdominal contractions required for defecation.
emphasis: The first urge to defecate is felt when rectal pressure reaches about 18 mmHg

rationales.a: 12 mmHg is below the threshold cited in this source item.
rationales.b: 14 mmHg is below the source’s first-urge pressure.
rationales.c: 16 mmHg is slightly below the stated approximate value.
